subject: physics
question_text: Obtain the relation between temperature and volume for an adiabatic process.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Short Answer Question 10 (printed p.130). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: combining PV^γ = constant with PV = nRT gives P = nRT/V, and substituting back gives nR T V^(γ−1) = constant, so T V^(γ−1) = constant since n and R are fixed; applied to two states this gives T₁V₁^(γ−1) = T₂V₂^(γ−1), so an adiabatic expansion (V increases) cools the gas and an adiabatic compression (V decreases) heats it.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Starting point
lines: and every state of an ideal gas
so P can be written as
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write both PV^γ = constant and PV = nRT before combining them.
steps.why: The T–V relation has to come from combining the adiabatic condition with the equation of state — neither one alone contains temperature and volume together.
common_mistakes: Starting straight from PV^γ = constant without also writing PV = nRT.
Writing P = nRT/V incorrectly as P = nR/(TV) or similar.

recall.must_convey: That the derivation starts from P V to the gamma equals constant and P V equals n R T, giving P equals n R T over V.
accept: P V to the gamma equals constant
P V equals n R T
P equals n R T over V
reject: T V to the gamma minus one equals constant
heard_as: P equals n R T over V

steps.memory_tip: Two relations are needed here, not one: the adiabatic condition AND the gas equation.

steps.label: Substituting
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Substitute and simplify the power of V to (γ − 1).
steps.why: Substituting removes P from the relation, leaving only the temperature and the volume — which is exactly what the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Cancelling V incorrectly and losing the power (γ − 1).
Forgetting that V^γ / V = V^(γ−1), not V^γ itself.

recall.must_convey: That substituting P equals n R T over V into P V to the gamma equals constant gives n R times T V to the gamma minus one equals constant.
accept: substitute n R T over V
T V to the gamma minus one
power drops to gamma minus one
reject: P equals n R T over V

steps.memory_tip: V^γ divided by V leaves V to the power (γ − 1) — one V has cancelled, not all of them.

steps.label: The relation
lines: Since n and R are themselves
into the constant on the right,
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The boxed relation TV^(γ−1) = constant.
steps.why: n and R never change during the process, so dropping them into the constant is valid and gives the cleanest form of the result.
common_mistakes: Leaving nR explicitly in the final boxed relation instead of absorbing it.
Writing the power as γ instead of (γ − 1).

recall.must_convey: That n and R are constants, so T V to the power gamma minus one equals constant.
accept: T V to the gamma minus one equals constant
n and R absorbed into the constant
reject: T one V one to the gamma minus one equals T two V two to the gamma minus one
heard_as: T V gamma minus one equals constant

steps.memory_tip: The final relation has NO n and NO R in it — both are absorbed into the constant.

steps.label: What it means
lines: Between an initial and a final
increases, so T must fall: the gas
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Apply the relation to two states and state both directions.
steps.why: The relation on its own is just algebra — the physical content is that a bigger V on one side must be balanced by a smaller T, which is the cooling-on-expansion result used throughout this chapter.
common_mistakes: Stating the relation but never saying which direction the temperature moves.
Getting expansion and compression backwards — expansion COOLS, it does not heat.

recall.must_convey: That applying the relation to two states gives T one V one to the gamma minus one equals T two V two to the gamma minus one, so expansion cools the gas and compression heats it.
accept: T one V one to the gamma minus one equals T two V two to the gamma minus one
reject: T V to the gamma minus one equals constant

steps.memory_tip: Bigger V, smaller T: V and T move opposite ways in TV^(γ−1) = constant.

insider_note: TV^(γ−1) = constant has no n or R in it — an answer that leaves them in has not finished simplifying the third mark.
